documents.title: Faculty FAQs: Artificial Intelligence
documents.summary: An academic-integrity office FAQ for faculty. It says there is no university-wide AI ban, that instructors set expectations, that detectors are not recommended, and suggests meeting students and redesigning assessments; it also lists faculty development.
documents.stance_why: The FAQ says "Faculty have the discretion to set expectations for AI use in their courses" and "there is no University-wide ban on AI tools", so it sets no stance itself and hands the decision to instructors: delegates.

units.anchor: hosting the first AI Summit in Spring 2023
units.policy: UNC Charlotte hosted the first AI Summit in Spring 2023 and continues to bring faculty and academic leaders together to build shared understanding and consistent guidance.
units.fit_note: Campus convenings of faculty and leaders rather than external coalitions.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B found this. The source says the university hosted 'the first AI Summit in Spring 2023' and keeps bringing faculty and leaders together to build shared guidance; it is a statement about institutional engagement, so it is kept.

documents.title: Suggested Syllabus Policies & Notices
tiers: Option 1: generative AI permitted in all assignments, with disclosure and attribution
Option 2: generative AI permitted only on instructor-designated assignments, with disclosure and attribution
documents.summary: A legal-affairs page of suggested syllabus language. Its AI section tells faculty to state when AI may be used and gives two optional policies (permit everywhere with attribution, or only on designated assignments with attribution), plus guidance on AI-detection tools and student consent.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no single rule; it says faculty "should notify students how and when generative AI tools" may be used and offers "two suggested syllabus policies ... depending on the level of generative AI use the faculty member wants to permit". It hands the decision to instructors and lists two tiers, so delegates.

units.why: The page says faculty 'should notify students how and when generative AI tools' may be used; a best-practice recommendation to instructors to communicate AI expectations, so P09 with actor instructor, course-start, should.
units.anchor: faculty members should notify students how and when generative AI tools
units.policy: Faculty should notify students how and when generative AI tools may be used in their assignments, exams, and other course work.

units.why: The two suggested policies are offered 'depending on the level of generative AI use the faculty member wants to permit', so the university sets no rule but gives a menu of levels; this is P05 (named options) while the choice rests with the instructor.
units.anchor: two suggested syllabus policies that may be used or adapted
units.policy: Two suggested syllabus policies, adaptable to the level of generative AI use the faculty member wants to permit, are offered.
units.resolution_why: Coder A set modality informs; coder B set may. The page only offers two suggested policies that 'may be used or adapted'; it does not give a permission to anyone, so informs.

units.why: The page says the Office of Student Accountability "provides a number of resources for faculty", including guidance on "setting expectations for the use of AI" and "sample disclosure language"; this is support for faculty setting policy (P63).
units.anchor: guidance related to setting expectations for the use of AI
units.frag_start: In addition, the Office of Student Accountability
units.frag_end: account for how AI is used
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this. The source says the Office of Student Accountability and Conflict Resolution provides 'guidance related to setting expectations for the use of AI through syllabus statements', a resource for faculty, so it is kept.

units.why: Option 1 text: 'students are permitted to use generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools like Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini'; default permission for all course work, so P02.
units.anchor: students are permitted to use generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools
units.policy: In this course, students are permitted to use generative AI tools like Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini to support their work.

units.why: The template says students 'must disclose any AI-generated material they use and properly attribute it'; a disclosure and attribution duty, P24.
units.anchor: students must disclose any AI-generated material they use and properly attribute it
units.policy: Students must disclose any AI-generated material they use and properly attribute it, including in-text citations, quotations, and references.
units.resolution_why: Coder A set unit stance permit; coder B set require. 'Students must disclose any AI-generated material they use' is a condition on permitted AI use, not a requirement to use AI, so permit.

units.why: "students are responsible for any errors or information that is misrepresented or inaccurate (i.e. hallucinations)" makes students own what AI contributes to submitted work. P29 (own what you submit) is chosen over P31 because the passage assigns responsibility rather than telling students to verify.
units.anchor: students are responsible for any errors or information that is misrepresented or inaccurate (i.e. hallucinations)
units.frag_start: Be aware that students are responsible
units.policy: Students are responsible for any errors or inaccurate information (hallucinations) that generative AI tools produce when they submit work that includes AI-generated material.
units.resolution_why: Coder A chose P29; coder B chose P31 (verify output) with a fit note that it is about accountability. 'Students are responsible for any errors or information that is misrepresented or inaccurate' says who owns the output, not that they must check it, so P29. B's note: it stresses that students bear responsibility for AI errors in submitted work, not only that output may be wrong. Notes from the coders not carried onto the unit: coder B fit note: Stresses that students bear responsibility for AI errors in submitted work (accountability), not only that output may be wrong..

units.why: The template supplies an exact 'acknowledges the use of [generative AI tool Name]' statement naming the tool and how it was used; P25 (tool and manner details) fits better than generic P24.
units.anchor: acknowledges the use of [generative AI tool Name] in the preparation or completion
units.policy: Students include in their assignments a statement acknowledging the generative AI tool used and the way(s) it was used (for example brainstorming, grammatical correction, citation, which portion).
units.fit_note: Template statement names the tool and how it was used (e.g. brainstorming, grammatical correction); it does not ask for the exact prompt or output. / Requires tool name and manner of use, not prompt or output.
units.resolution_why: Coder A set unit stance permit; coder B set require. The acknowledgement statement is the disclosure condition on permitted use, not required AI use, so permit. Both coders gave P25 with a fit note; both notes are kept.

units.why: The note warns that "the data you supply might be used for training AI models" and tells students to "avoid sharing any sensitive or private information", a data-protection rule (P50) addressed to students.
units.anchor: avoid sharing any sensitive or private information when using these tools
units.frag_start: You should exercise caution and avoid sharing
units.policy: Students should avoid sharing sensitive or private information (personally identifiable information, PHI, financial data, intellectual property, original research, legally protected data) with generative AI tools, because supplied data might be used for training and confidentiality is not guaranteed.
units.resolution_why: Coder A set modality should-not; coder B set should. 'Avoid sharing any sensitive or private information' is a request not to do something, so should-not. B's fuller policy wording is kept; it follows the source.

units.why: Option 2 notes faculty 'should specifically indicate on each assignment whether generative AI is permitted, and the way in which it may be used'; an instruction to instructors to state expectations in assignment instructions, P09.
units.anchor: specifically indicate on each assignment whether generative AI is permitted
units.policy: Faculty members should specifically indicate on each assignment whether generative AI is permitted, and the way in which it may be used.

units.why: Option 2 limits AI to 'only for specific assignments, and only as designated by the instructor'; permission is per assignment, so the instructor sets the rule (P04). It is not P01 since AI is allowed where designated.
units.anchor: only for specific assignments, and only as designated by the instructor
units.policy: In this course, students are permitted to use generative AI tools only for specific assignments, and only as designated by the instructor.

units.why: The phrase 'use of a generative AI tool that is not specifically authorized by the instructor may constitute a violation of the Code of Student Academic Integrity' classifies unauthorized AI use as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: not specifically authorized by the instructor may constitute a violation of the
units.policy: Use of a generative AI tool that is not specifically authorized by the instructor may constitute a violation of the Code of Student Academic Integrity.

units.why: 'Use of SimCheck ... is entirely in the discretion of the instructor' but needs advance syllabus notice and signed consent. This concerns plagiarism detection, not AI, and no type covers consent to plagiarism tools, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: entirely in the discretion of the instructor
units.policy: Use of SimCheck or another plagiarism detection service is entirely in the discretion of the instructor, but requires advance notice in the syllabus and a signed consent form from each student.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors must give students advance syllabus notice that plagiarism or AI detection services will be used. / Instructors who use SimCheck or other plagiarism detection must give advance syllabus notice and obtain signed student consent (plagiarism tools, not AI-specific).
units.resolution_why: The coders gave different unit stances (A neutral, B restrict). The sentence sets conditions on the instructor's use of SimCheck or another plagiarism service, which is not student AI use, so neutral. Both coders marked it UNCOVERED and both notes are kept.

units.why: The detection section says tools like ZeroGPT are 'designated as DO NOT USE by OneIT' as they are error-prone and fail reliability standards; detectors are unreliable and should not be used, P39.
units.anchor: designated as DO NOT USE by OneIT
units.policy: Generative AI detection tools (such as ZeroGPT) are designated DO NOT USE by OneIT because no University enterprise tool is available or recommended.

units.why: The text says detection products 'are prone to error and do not meet reliability standards' and do not ensure privacy; this is the reasoning behind the ban and a statement of unreliability (P39); the privacy part is the fit note.
units.anchor: prone to error and do not meet reliability standards
units.policy: Both free and paid generative AI detection products are prone to error and do not meet reliability standards.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B had the reliability point as its own unit; coder A coded only the privacy half. Coder B's unit merged two points, so it is trimmed to the reliability point and the privacy point stays in coder A's unit. Notes from the coders not carried onto the unit: coder B fit note: Also says detection tools do not sufficiently protect the privacy of content entered into them..

units.why: The page states detectors "often do not sufficiently ensure the privacy of any data or content that is input into them", a data-privacy reason against uploading student work, so P50 (protect data, prefer vetted tools).
units.anchor: do not sufficiently ensure the privacy of any data or content
units.frag_start: Moreover, such products often do not
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this (coder B joined it with the reliability point in one unit). The source says detection products 'often do not sufficiently ensure the privacy of any data or content that is input into them', a separate privacy point, so it is kept.

units.why: 'such tools should not be relied on as presumptive of the use of generative AI' sets an evidence standard: detector output is not presumptive proof, which fits P69 (detector output not proof) better than P39 because it speaks to what counts as evidence.
units.anchor: should not be relied on as presumptive of the use of generative AI
units.policy: Generative AI detection tools should not be relied on as presumptive of the use of generative AI in completing an assignment.

units.why: Instructors who use a detector 'against University recommendations' must 'obtain a signed consent' to notify students and obtain FERPA consent and copyright permission; a consent condition on detection. No type is about student consent to detection tools, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: obtain a signed consent before submitting student work to a generative AI detection tool
units.policy: Before submitting student work to a generative AI detection tool, an instructor obtains a signed consent that notifies students of the tool and provides FERPA consent and copyright permission.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors must notify students and obtain signed FERPA and copyright consent before submitting student work to an AI detection tool. / Instructors must notify students and obtain signed FERPA and copyright consent before uploading their work to AI detection or plagiarism tools.
units.resolution_why: Coder A set modality must; coder B set should. 'It is important to obtain a signed consent' is advice for instructors who choose to use a detector against recommendations, so should.

documents.title: Office of Undergraduate Research AI policy
documents.summary: A unit policy for undergraduate research sponsored by the Office of Undergraduate Research. AI may assist with research, writing and presentations with mentor approval and disclosure, but the student must understand and defend the work and may not use AI for full content or fabricated data.
documents.stance_why: The policy says 'AI-generated content may be used as a tool to assist in the writing or research processes' and lists acceptable uses, with conditions: 'documented prior approval from their faculty mentor', disclosure, and no full generation of sections. Use is allowed under conditions, and the list of acceptable uses is given as examples, so permit rather than restrict (coder B chose restrict).

units.why: The policy says 'the responsibility for the work, learning, validity, authenticity, and accuracy always lies with the human researcher', putting ownership on the human; P29.
units.anchor: the responsibility for the work, learning, validity, authenticity, and accuracy
units.policy: The responsibility for the work, learning, validity, authenticity, and accuracy always lies with the human researcher.
units.resolution_why: Coder A set actor student; coder B set all. 'The responsibility for the work ... always lies with the human researcher' covers students and mentors in OUR-sponsored research, so all.

units.why: 'Generative AI is not, and cannot be, a substitute for the human endeavor in creating and learning' says AI must not replace human thinking, P32.
units.anchor: Generative AI is not, and cannot be, a substitute for the human endeavor
units.policy: Generative AI is not, and cannot be, a substitute for the human endeavor in creating and learning.
units.resolution_why: Coder A set actor student; coder B set all. The principle covers every researcher in OUR programs, so all.

units.why: The policy notes AI's "unintended negative consequences on the environment, generating and disseminating misinformation", naming harms (P53).
units.anchor: use of AI has unintended negative consequences on the environment, generating and disseminating misinformation
units.frag_start: the use of AI has unintended negative consequences

new_types.name: Notify students and obtain consent before submitting their work to a detector
new_types.definition: Instructors tell students in the syllabus and get signed consent before uploading student work to a plagiarism or AI detection service.

new_types.name: Require mentor approval before AI use
new_types.definition: Students must get documented prior approval from a faculty mentor or supervisor before using AI in a project.

notes: Scope: all four included documents are university-layer and aimed at faculty or employees; no college or computing unit policy exists. Syllabus page is mostly unrelated syllabus boilerplate; only the AI section, AI-detection notice and consent rules were coded. Option 2 repeats Option 1's disclosure and data-protection text; those exact repeats were not coded again. General syllabus lines (violation penalties, proof assignments are own work, recording bans) were skipped as not AI-specific. FAQ and syllabus page say detectors should not be relied on, yet the syllabus page supplies template language for detector use with consent. Candidate new types: mentor/supervisor approval before AI use (OUR); consent and notice before detector use (syllabus page). Reconciler: all four documents are university-layer; no school or computing-unit policy was found by either coder. Syllabus page: B's units on generic syllabus penalties (P37) and prohibited third-party materials (CourseHero, Chegg) were dropped as not AI-specific. OUR and OneIT document stances were reconciled to permit (see each stance_why). Candidate new types come from coder A's notes. Coder B's note: OneIT guidelines are written for employees, so most units have actor all.
